about: How the Guarani of 2.º grado, unit 3 («Aikotevẽ») was written: two independent drafts (MEC fidelity; how a child says it), a merge, and three independent checks of every string (spelling and syllables; meaning and grammar; usage, register and attestation). All three passed every string, so «final» is the merge unchanged and is the unit as it is in project/tp-grades.js.

drafts.notes:
My angle was fidelity to the MEC capacity. I read the capacity in the MEC texts and built every card on the app's words and on frames the child already knows.

THE CAPACITY
- Priorización curricular 2021, Comunicación Guaraní (the L2 table), 2.º grado, item 16 (PDF p. 28, in docs/mec-check.json): «Expresa necesidades básicas como: ir al baño, tomar agua, pedir alimentos, solicitar permiso y prestar algo.»
- The same sentence is in the MEC's Programa de estudio for 2.º grado, Segunda lengua, Expresión oral (scratchpad mec-text/7e820984-Pages_from_4933.txt, l. 3336, p. 57).
- Guía para la planificación de clases 2021, Comunicación Guaraní, Segundo grado, week 4 (26–29 April), «Necesidades básicas» (mec-text/25531b74-…, l. 2707–2711, p. 59). It asks for picture cards of the needs, example situations, and practice between peers.
- No MEC text gives Guarani wording for these needs. The corpus has no baño, y'u or vare'a, so the Guarani is mine.

THE FIVE NEEDS IN THREE SCHOOL MOMENTS
- Night 1 «Chevare'a», at the merienda, with the teacher: tomar agua (Chey'uhéi, tengo sed) and pedir alimentos (Chevare'a; Eme'ẽmína chéve mbujape).
  - Say: Mbo'ehára, chevare'a. / Ejapyhy ko mbujape. / Aguyje!
- Night 2 «Ikatúpa asẽ?», in class, with the teacher: solicitar permiso for the body's needs.
  - ir al baño: Ikatúpa asẽ sapy'aite?
  - tomar agua: Ikatúpa hay'u?
  - eating one's snack: Ikatúpa ha'u che chipa?
  - Say: Ikatúpa asẽ sapy'aite? / Héẽ, ikatu. / Aguyje, mbo'ehára.
- Night 3 «Ejapyhy», in class, between classmates: prestar algo.
  - The classmate needs an eraser: Aikotevẽ peteĩ mbogueha.
  - The child lends its own: Ejapyhy che mbogueha.
  - The child asks for it back: Upéi eme'ẽ jey chéve. Asking for it back is what makes it a loan and not a gift.
  - Cards: mbogueha, Ejapyhy, Eiporu che haiha.
- How this matches the guide:
  - Every card is a picture card of a need (the guide's «fichas con imágenes»).
  - Each say set is a need and its answer.
  - Night 3 is the «práctica entre pares».
  - The unit title Aikotevẽ (necesito) is said by the classmate in night 3.

BUILT ON 1.º GRADO UNIT 5 (NO CARD REPEATED) AND 2.º GRADO UNIT 2
- The frame Ikatúpa + a-verb? gets three new verbs: asẽ, hay'u and ha'u. «Héẽ, ikatu.» answers it the way «Héẽ, eike.» did. Night 2 ends with unit 5's own «Aguyje, mbo'ehára.».
- Eme'ẽmína chéve… now asks for food (mbujape) instead of paper.
- ejapyhy moves from unit 5's say line («Héẽ, ejapyhy.») to a card, and now the child is the one who hands something over.
- aiporu becomes eiporu. In 1.º grado the child asked «Ikatúpa aiporu nde haiha?»; now it lends: «Eiporu che haiha».
- These words keep the meanings they have in the app:
  - y 'agua': its water drop is the picture for Chey'uhéi and Ikatúpa hay'u?, and the y is inside both words.
  - mbujape 'pan', chipa 'chipá', haiha 'lápiz', mbo'ehára, Héẽ, Aguyje.
  - peteĩ 'uno', here 'un'.
  - upéi, as on the «Upéi» button, and jey, as in «Eha'ã jey».

THE BATHROOM QUESTION
Choice: «Ikatúpa asẽ sapy'aite?» (¿Puedo salir un ratito?), with a toilet picture and the gloss «(para ir al baño)». Reasons:
1. Guarani has no common noun for the school toilet.
   - The dictionary forms I found are jahuha (a place to bathe) and koty'i ('cuartito'), in the Avañe'ẽ dictionary of the Argentine MEC, through a search summary. I found neither used for a school bathroom.
   - Speakers use the Spanish noun. A copy of Wikipedia's Jopara article gives «Mo'o opyta baño?» as its example of a Spanish word inside Guarani. Paraguayología notes that the room is simply called «baño» (jahu is 'bañarse').
2. The loanword cannot be written in this app as it stands.
   - b is not one of the 33 letters of the achegety. By a search summary, it is also not among the letters the Academia later admitted for loanwords (d, f, ll).
   - The app's own audit (docs/guarani-audit.json) rejected the Spanish spelling «Castellano» for that reason. It also rejected «Mba'e vocal-pe oñepyrũ?», because a Spanish word with a hyphen «should not be used as written».
   - A guaranized «váño» appears in no source I checked.
   - So «Ikatúpa aha baño-pe?» would fail the app's own check.
3. The register rule asks for Guarani where a common Guarani form exists, and one exists for the whole request.
   - «Ikatúpa asẽ sapy'aite» is attested as a permission request in «Guaraní Comunicativo en la Función Pública», the Paraguayan civil-service course. 1.º grado unit 5's usage lens found it (docs/unit5-check.json).
   - It is unit 5's frame with one new verb.
   - It is how a child politely leaves the room for the bathroom, just as «¿Puedo salir?» is in Spanish.
4. The need is still named, as the MEC asks: by the picture (a toilet) and by the gloss «¿Puedo salir un ratito? (para ir al baño)». The parenthesis follows the app's «Me llamo… (decí tu nombre)».
Fallback, if teachers want the room named: «Ikatúpa aha baño-pe?», which is what most families say. It needs a team decision on putting a Spanish noun in a Guarani card, and a new clip.

PICTURES
- Existing: y, mbujape, chipa, haiha.
- New, 4 (the maximum): vare'a (hungry child), baño (toilet), mbogueha (eraser), ejapyhy (a hand passing a notebook). The notebook keeps the handing picture apart from night 3's pencil and eraser.
- Pictures are distinct within each night. y appears in nights 1 and 2 and is also unit 2's y. The engine never shows two cards with the same picture together.

CHECKED IN MEMORY
I used the real project/tp-course.js, with the unit inserted as 2.º grado unit 3 and the later units renumbered. No file was written.
- Syllables:
  - Che·y·'u·héi, Che·va·re·'a, mbo·gue·ha and E·ja·py·hy join back to their words.
  - Every syllable ends in a vowel, mb and gu stay whole, and the puso begins its syllable.
  - Phrases have [], and nights 1 and 3 each have 2 items with syl.
  - All strings are NFC with the ASCII puso.
- Games:
  - L1: meet+read+build | meet+read+pairs | meet+read+build.
  - L2 and BI: meet+pick+say | meet+read+say | meet+pick+say.
- Distractors: I tested 9 cards with 60 seeds, using both Pick's and Check's seeds (1,080 sets). No set holds two cards with the same picture.
- Clips: 17 keys, 15 of them new.
  - «Ikatúpa asẽ sapy'aite?» shares its card's clip.
  - «Aguyje!» and «Aguyje, mbo'ehára.» already have clips in the 1.º grado pack.
- Length: the longest cards, «Eme'ẽmína chéve mbujape» and «Ikatúpa ha'u che chipa?», have 23 characters. The app's longest now has 25.

TO SETTLE OUTSIDE THE UNIT
- Ñandu Pysã has 5 stars in tp-sky.js, and 2.º grado already has 5 units (2 written, 3 announced). A sixth unit gets no star unless the figure gets one more star or two units merge. The same thing happened with Eichu in 1.º grado.
- The g2 «can» text in tp-grades.js does not mention needs (its «mec» text does).

EVIDENCE OUTSIDE THE APP
- Tatoeba copy (dl-biling/grn.csv):
  - «Ndevare'a piko?» (l. 694), «Hey'u.» (l. 667), «Eme'ẽmíkena chéve che hay'urã» (l. 887), «Ha'use peteĩ mba'e he'ẽva» (l. 882).
  - «Ko jagua imorotĩ» (l. 200), «reju jey» (l. 81), oikotevẽ (l. 94, 299), «Ikatu apoko?» (l. 439).
- USC Guarani Corpus: hay'ú (1Sg.drink) and hoy'u (3Pl). Wikipedia: 'I drink water' is pronounced hay'u.
- Glosbe: «Cheyuhéi, aháta aheka y potĩ». La Nación (14-06-2025): «che vare'a» (tengo hambre).
- mbogueha: Avañe'ẽ dictionary, Glosbe, Paraguayología.
- Limits: WebFetch could not reach dokumen.pub or www.mec.gob.ar, which are outside this session's network. I saw those sources, and the other web items above, only through search summaries. Reading them directly needs those hosts allowed in the session's network settings.

doubts.doubt: The bathroom card does not name the bathroom; the toilet picture and the gloss «(para ir al baño)» do. Most Guarani-speaking families use the Spanish noun («Ikatúpa aha baño-pe?»), and a reviewer may prefer it. That needs a team decision first: b is not in the achegety, the app's audit rejected a Spanish word with a hyphen, and «váño» appears in no source I checked. The attestation of «Ikatúpa asẽ sapy'aite» comes from 1.º grado unit 5's usage lens, from the Función Pública course on dokumen.pub. I could not open it to check (the host is outside this session's network). sapy'a alone can mean 'de repente' (the USC corpus glosses it 'suddenly'); in this request, with -ite, it is 'un ratito'. The synthetic voice has garbled short nasal words, so check «asẽ» in the clip.

I wrote hay'u, not ay'u: the 1sg of y'u is irregular, like ha'u. Evidence: USC Guarani Corpus hay'ú and hoy'u; Wikipedia gives 'I drink water' as pronounced hay'u; Tatoeba has «Hey'u.». Some teachers write «ay'u», so please confirm the Academia's form. In the same night it sounds close to «Ikatúpa ha'u che chipa?» (hay'u / ha'u). In night 2, L2 and BI read rather than listen, and «che chipa» tells the two apart, but the big star's listening game could put them side by side.

I wrote it joined, as the person marker of a stative predicate (Tatoeba «Ndevare'a piko?»). Others write «Che y'uhéi» or «cheyuhéi». The split Che·y·'u·héi keeps y as its own syllable, as the app's y·pe does; a teacher who reads «ey» as a diphthong would split it differently. Many children would rather say «Hay'use» (quiero tomar agua). It reuses unit 2's water drop, so a child may at first take the card for «y».

Joined, as in Tatoeba («Ndevare'a piko?»), but La Nación writes «che vare'a». In this one unit, L1 readers meet the possessive che written apart (che haiha, che mbogueha, che chipa) and this che- written joined, as in the app's Chepytyvõ. The new picture must read as hungry, not as a tummy ache.

It is in the Avañe'ẽ dictionary of the Argentine MEC («borrador. m. Mbogueha, mboje'oha»), in Glosbe and in Paraguayología. I saw all three only through search summaries (www.mec.gob.ar is outside this session's network). Many children just say «borrador» or «goma» in Spanish. As far as I know, the gloss «borrador» is the Paraguayan word; «goma (de borrar)» is the alternative.

Night 3 lends with everyday verbs, Ejapyhy (tomá) and Eiporu (usá), and marks the loan with «Upéi eme'ẽ jey chéve». It avoids poruka, the dictionary verb for 'prestar': 1.º grado unit 5's check found poruka in no Paraguayan sentence and replaced it. If the team wants the MEC's verb itself, use «Aiporuka ndéve che mbogueha» (Te presto mi borrador). It takes ndéve for the receiver, not ro-, because the object is the thing lent, as chéve was in «Reiporukápa chéve nde haiha?». The new handing picture is somewhat abstract; check that children read it as 'tomá'.

The whole line is unattested. It is built from app words: upéi (the «Upéi» button), jey («Eha'ã jey»), eme'ẽ and chéve (1.º grado). jey means 'back' as in Tatoeba's «reju jey». «Embojevy chéve» (devolvémelo) is the other form; I could not confirm which one teachers prefer.

The whole sentence is unattested, though its parts are attested (ha'u, as in Tatoeba «Ha'use…»; unit 2's chipa). Children ask to eat their snack in class at merienda time, but less often than they ask for the bathroom or water. If the team prefers a permission that is not about food, «Ikatúpa aipe'a ovetã?» (¿Puedo abrir la ventana?, picture ovetã) fits the same slot. The 1.º grado usage lens suggested it.

«ko mbujape» (este pan) follows Tatoeba's «Ko jagua imorotĩ»; «Ejapyhy peteĩ mbujape» (tomá un pan) is just as natural. The say set has the child state the need (Chevare'a) rather than say the card's «Eme'ẽmína chéve mbujape», to keep each line under ten syllables.

In Tatoeba, aikotevẽ takes its object directly («Opavave oikotevẽ pirapire») and also with -re («oikotevẽ ikafére»); I used the plain object. The unit title Aikotevẽ is said only here. «Ndaguerekói mbogueha» (No tengo borrador), from the app's aguereko, is another way for the classmate to state the need. The voice has trouble with final nasals (Aikotevẽ, asẽ, Héẽ), so check those clips first.

This is the plain answer to Ikatúpa…?. A teacher may add «Tereho ha ejevy pya'e» (andá y volvé rápido); I left it out to keep the line short. tereho is the standard imperative of ho (Tatoeba «Tereho ko'ãga»), though «eho» is also heard. Héẽ keeps 1.º grado unit 5's spelling, which is still to be confirmed with the Academia.

«Usá mi lápiz» lends by letting someone use the pencil, which is how children lend, but the verb is 'usar', not 'prestar' (see Ejapyhy). Eiporu is in the MEC teacher guides; the Priorización also writes puru (Oipuru), so some children will hear «Eipuru».
«Maestra» follows the app's gloss of mbo'ehára, as in 1.º grado unit 5; children often say «Profe».

words.note: y'u 'tomar agua' (y + 'u) + -se 'querer'. The 1st person ahy'u follows the school paradigm the app already uses for hoy'u in the Mborevi Rape story (ahy'u, rehy'u, hoy'u). Same picture as unit 2's y.
karu 'comer' + -se; Tatoeba has the negative Ndakaruséi. Ahy'use and Akaruse share -se = «quiero», so in L1 the child builds two words with the same ending. Unit 2's bread stands for food to eat.
1.º grado's frame («Eme'ẽmína chéve kuatia») with unit 2's kamby: asking for food at the merienda escolar, which in Paraguay is milk.

drafts.notes:
ANGLE: how a Paraguayan child really says it. Each card is the shortest everyday form a Guarani-speaking teacher or family uses with a 7-year-old. Each night ends in a need-and-answer dialogue, and the child says both roles. This was a read-only task: no project file was touched (git status is clean). Scratch files: g2u3/draft.js (the unit) and g2u3/check.js (the engine check).

MEC FIT
Sources:
- Priorización curricular 2021, Comunicación Guaraní, 2.º grado, item 16 (p. 28): «Expresa necesidades básicas como: ir al baño, tomar agua, pedir alimentos, solicitar permiso y prestar algo.»
- Guía para la planificación 2021, 1.er ciclo, Comunicación Guaraní, Segundo grado, week 4 «Necesidades básicas» (p. 59).

The three nights:
- Night 1, the merienda, with the teacher. Tomar agua (Ahy'use) and pedir alimentos (Akaruse; Eme'ẽmína chéve kamby, the milk of the merienda escolar). Dialogue: Mbo'ehára, akaruse. → Ejapyhy ko mbujape. → Aguyje!
- Night 2, in class, with the teacher. Ir al baño and solicitar permiso, all in 1.º grado's frame Ikatúpa + a-verb?: asẽ sapy'aite (bathroom), ahy'u (water), akaru (eating). Dialogue: Ikatúpa asẽ sapy'aite? → Héẽ, tereho.
- Night 3, in class, with a classmate. Prestar algo, with the child as the lender: the classmate states the need (Aikotevẽ haiha), and the child answers Ejapyhy (tomá) and Eiporu (usalo). Dialogue: Che irũ, aikotevẽ haiha. → Ejapyhy che haiha. → Aguyjevete!

The guide's three activities:
- «Fichas con imágenes» are the picture cards (Meet, Pick/Read).
- «Situaciones» are the three scenes.
- «Práctica entre pares» is Say, where the child plays both roles; night 3 happens between classmates.

THE BATHROOM QUESTION
Decision: the Guarani paraphrase «Ikatúpa asẽ sapy'aite?» (¿Puedo salir un ratito?), on a new toilet picture, glossed «¿Puedo salir un ratito? (al baño)». Evidence:
1. Everyday speech uses the Spanish loan. English Wikipedia's Jopara article gives «Mo'o opyta baño?» ('Where is the bathroom?') as its example of mixed speech. So baño is jopara, not school Guarani.
2. I found no Guarani noun for the toilet room anywhere I looked:
   - the MEC texts (baño appears only in Spanish)
   - the 987 Tatoeba pairs
   - docs/unit5-check.json and docs/guarani-audit.json
   - web searches for jahuha and tekotevẽha
   Jahuha would mean 'place to bathe', not the toilet. Either word would be a purist coinage, which the brief rules out.
3. The paraphrase is attested as a polite permission request in «Guaraní Comunicativo en la Función Pública», found by the previous check (docs/unit5-check.json, usage lens). Every part is everyday Guarani:
   - asẽ: Tatoeba «Asẽkuri javete»; the MEC 5.º grado guide «osẽ hag̃ua»
   - sapy'a + the tonic -ite
   - the frame Ikatúpa
   It mirrors 1.º grado's «Ikatúpa aike?»: aike 'entro', asẽ 'salgo'.
4. In Paraguayan classrooms, «¿Puedo salir?» is the usual polite way to ask for the bathroom, in Spanish too. The picture and the gloss name the place.
5. In 2.º grado the child reads and builds the card, right before the consonants unit. The loan would bring in b, which is not a Guarani letter (it only appears in mb). How Guarani writes an unadapted loan with a suffix (baño-pe or bañope) is also unsettled.
The loan stays in doubts as the fallback.

WATER
The app already writes the 3rd person hoy'u (tp-sky.js), from the audit's school paradigm (Guasch & Ortiz: ahy'u, rehy'u, hoy'u). So the 1st person is ahy'u (Ahy'use, Ikatúpa ahy'u?). Speech also has ay'u (see doubts).

BUILT ON 1.º GRADO, UNIT 5 (no card repeated)
- The frame Ikatúpa + a-verb gets three new verbs: asẽ, ahy'u, akaru.
- «Eme'ẽmína chéve kuatia» becomes «Eme'ẽmína chéve kamby».
- 1.º grado's «Héẽ, ejapyhy.» (the line where a classmate lent the pencil) becomes the card Ejapyhy and the child's own «Ejapyhy che haiha.».
- «Ikatúpa aiporu nde haiha?» becomes Eiporu.
- Héẽ, Aguyje and Aguyjevete close the dialogues.
New grammar is small:
- the desiderative -se, shared by Ahy'use and Akaruse (the two words night 1 builds)
- the imperative tereho
- aikotevẽ, the unit's title verb

REUSE AND PICTURES
Reused words keep their meanings in the app:
- from unit 2: y 'agua', kamby 'leche', mbujape 'pan'
- from 1.º grado: haiha 'lápiz', irũ, mbo'ehára, Aguyje, Aguyjevete
Existing pictures: y, mbujape, kamby, haiha. New pictures: 3 (baño, ejapyhy, eiporu), all on free keys.

ENGINE CHECK
I ran the unit in memory through the real tp-course.js, inserted as 2.º grado unit 3, with Pundie, Moõpa? and Purahéi ha kũjererã moved to units 4–6.
- Every string is NFC, with the ASCII puso and no ¿.
- The four syl lists join exactly: A·hy·'u·se, A·ka·ru·se, E·ja·py·hy, Ei·po·ru.
- Games per night:
  - Night 1: L1 meet+read+build (builds Ahy'use and Akaruse); L2 and BI meet+pick+say.
  - Night 2: L1 meet+read+pairs (the three Ikatúpa cards); L2 and BI meet+read+say.
  - Night 3: L1 meet+read+build (Ejapyhy, Eiporu); L2 and BI meet+pick+say.
- Pictures differ within each night. y and mbujape each serve one card in night 1 and one in night 2 (the need, then the permission). The engine never shows two cards with the same picture together, so these never meet each other or unit 2's y, mbujape and kamby cards.

The 1st person of y'u 'tomar agua' varies. ahy'u is the school paradigm the app already follows for hoy'u. One audit reviewer gave ay'u, rey'u, hoy'u, and ay'u is also heard in speech. tereho is the everyday imperative of ho 'ir' (Tatoeba «Tereho ko'ãga.»; Biblia GPC, Éx 4:12, «Tereho katu»), but school materials also use eho. Héẽ is spelled as in 1.º grado; Tatoeba has both Héẽ and Hẽe. The synthetic voice has garbled short nasal words before, so check this clip.

«Ndaguerekói haiha» ('no tengo lápiz') is at least as common from a child. THE BATHROOM QUESTION
Choice: the Guarani paraphrase «Ikatúpa asẽ sapy'aite?» (¿Puedo salir un ratito?), on a new toilet picture, glossed «¿Puedo salir un ratito? (al baño)». Both drafts chose it independently. Reasons:
1. The everyday noun is the Spanish loan.
   - Wikipedia's Jopara article gives «Mo'o opyta baño?» as its example of mixed speech (both drafts, search summaries).
   - In the MEC texts, baño appears only in Spanish. It is in neither the Tatoeba copy nor docs/unit5-check.json.
2. No common Guarani noun for the school toilet turned up.
   - Dictionary forms such as jahuha ('place to bathe') or koty'i ('cuartito') are not used for it, and putting one on a card would be the purist coinage the brief rules out.
   - My searches in this step also found none: bilingual signage, the Secretaría de Políticas Lingüísticas, school phrase lists.
3. The loan cannot be written in the app as it stands.
   - b is not a letter of the achegety; it appears only inside mb.
   - The app's audit (docs/guarani-audit.json) rejected a Spanish spelling and a Spanish word written with a hyphen.
   - No guaranized form (váño) turned up. Tatoeba's hyphen («Tom-pe», «Boston-gui») is for foreign names.
4. The paraphrase is attested as a polite permission request.
   - «Ikatúpa asẽ sapy'aite» is in «Guaraní Comunicativo en la Función Pública», the Paraguayan civil-service course. 1.º grado unit 5's usage lens found it through a search summary (docs/unit5-check.json).
   - Its parts are everyday Guarani: asẽ (Tatoeba «Asẽkuri javete»), sapy'a with the tonic -ite, and the frame Ikatúpa.
   - It mirrors 1.º grado's «Ikatúpa aike?».
5. «¿Puedo salir?» is how Paraguayan children politely ask for the bathroom in Spanish too. The picture and the gloss name the place, which is what the guide's picture cards ask for.
6. Guarani's own verb for the need, kuaru 'orinar' (akuaruse), names a body function rather than asking politely, and my search found it in no school or phrase source. It is not used.

verdicts.general:
RESULT
- All 22 Guarani strings pass the spelling and syllable check: no fix and no drop.
- Nothing in the project was touched. My check script is g2u3-spell/spell.js, run on the merge's merged.js.

MECHANICAL CHECKS
- Every string is NFC, uses the ASCII puso (U+0027), and has no ¿ or ¡.
- Questions end in «?». Cards have no final period; say lines do.
- Syllables: the four syl lists (Ha·y·'u·se, A·ka·ru·se, mbo·gue·ha, E·ja·py·hy) join exactly to their words.
  - Every syllable ends in a vowel, mb and gu stay whole, and the puso begins its syllable.
  - All phrases have [].
- Shared words match tp-grades.js code point for code point: Eme'ẽmína, chéve, mbujape, mbo'ehára, Aguyje, Aguyjevete, Ikatúpa, Héẽ, ejapyhy, che, haiha, irũ.

ACCENTS
- Atonic suffixes in this unit: the question -pa (Ikatúpa), the dative -ve (chéve) and the request -na (in -mína).
- Tonic suffixes:
  - the desiderative -se (Hay'use, Akaruse). Tatoeba shows it with the acute on sé before an atonic suffix: Ahasékuri, Ndahaséi, Ndakaruséi, ja'eséva.
  - the intensifier -ite (sapy'aite). Tatoeba has ko'ãgaitépe.
  - -mi, -vete, the nominaliser -ha (mbogueha, like haiha) and -hára (stressed on há).
- So the only acutes in the unit are Ikatúpa, chéve, -mína, mbo'ehára and Héẽ, all written as the app already writes them.

WORD BOUNDARIES AND NASAL HARMONY
- Suffixes are joined to their word. The possessive che and the demonstrative ko are separate words; chéve is one word.
- No prefix in the unit has a nasal form that would apply: a-, e-, i- and che never change. The nasal forms would be ña-, ñe- or ne- (as in ñaikotevẽ, ñasẽ).
- The causative in mbogueha is mbo- because gue is oral.

THE WATER VERB
The evidence now clearly favours hay'u. From search summaries:
- Celso Ávalos' dictionary: «Che hay'u, nde rey'u, ha'e hoy'u».
- The GuaraniAyvuWeb dictionary lists hay'u and hoy'u.
- A Corrientes verb list gives hay'u/rey'u.
- English Wikipedia says 'a'y'u is pronounced hay'u.
- A grammar note gives jay'u.
Tatoeba fits the same paradigm: «Hey'u.» beside «He'u!», and «che hay'urã» beside «che ha'umirã».
No search found ahy'u. The app's audit (g290) cited it from Guasch & Ortiz without a quote, and its three reviewers disagreed with each other (one gave ay'u).
- A correction for the notes: «the h-forms of 'u (ha'u, he'u, ho'u)» should read ha'u, re'u, ho'u, with he'u as the imperative (Tatoeba «re'uete», «He'u!»). Likewise y'u is hay'u, rey'u, hoy'u, imperative hey'u.
- If the Academia ever gives ahy'u, the swap in the doubts is right: Ahy'use (A·hy·'u·se), with «Ikatúpa ahy'u?» and the night 1 title changed together.

SYLLABLES OF Hay'use
- a + y is not a diphthong: Guarani diphthongs end in i (es.wikipedia, «Fonología del guaraní»). So Ha·y is right, and the app already uses y as a syllable (y·pe).

MBOGUEHA
- This time I found it in Paraguayan sources (search summaries only):
  - David Galeano Olivera's children's lesson: «Borrador es mbogueha».
  - A Paraguayan school plan: «Mbogueha (Borrador)».
- Draft 1's «Avañe'ẽ» dictionary is the Corrientes (Argentina) one, so these two sources are better evidence.

BATHROOM FALLBACK SPELLING (not used in the unit)
- b is not a letter of the achegety. If the team chose the loan, its Guarani spelling would be «váño»:
  - v for b, as in Tatoeba's adapted «Víno» and «voleadóra»;
  - an acute because the stress is not on the last syllable;
  - -pe joined to it, like «mbo'ehaópe»: «Ikatúpa aha váñope?».
- Tatoeba uses a hyphen before -pe only after foreign proper names (Boston-pe, Tom-pe, Marruéko-pe).
- I found no source that writes «váño», so this only says how the word would be spelled.

STANDING CAVEATS (app-wide, unchanged)
- Héẽ (Tatoeba also has Hẽe) and the acute of -mína. If either changes, every string that uses it changes together.

LIMITS
- The web evidence is from search summaries only.
- Two hosts are outside this session's allowed network: kaweah.freedombox.rocks (a Wiktionary mirror with the y'u table) and guaranicorpus.usc.edu (the USC Guarani corpus). They would have to be allowed in the session's network settings before I could read them.

verdicts.general:
Result: all 22 Guarani strings are grammatical, and each one means what its Spanish says. Nothing needs a fix or a drop under this lens. Two items stay at medium confidence, for reasons of attestation, not grammar:
- The bathroom card, in its card and say lines. Its Guarani says only «¿Puedo salir un ratito?»; the bathroom is in the gloss's parenthesis and in the picture.
- mbogueha.
No file in the repository was changed.

What I checked:
- Person and mood:
  - Every request is a 1sg form: a- after the Ikatúpa frame (asẽ, hay'u, akaru), or 1sg + tonic -se (Hay'use, Akaruse).
  - Every answer or offer is a 2sg e- imperative for one listener (ejapyhy, eme'ẽ, eiporu).
  - i-verbs keep their i- (aikotevẽ, eiporu). japyhy and me'ẽ are not i-verbs, so they give ejapyhy and eme'ẽ.
  - The possessive che is written apart (che haiha, che mbogueha, che irũ). chéve marks the receiver of eme'ẽ, and ko + noun is the near demonstrative.
  - The unit uses no negation and no relational r-/h- noun.
- The water verb: hay'u has more support now than when the merge was written.
  - Earlier sources: Wikipedia, the USC corpus, and Tatoeba («Hey'u.», «che hay'urã»).
  - New, by search summary: a UNLP Guarani course page on irregular verbs and Ávalos's dictionary, both «che hay'u, nde rey'u, ha'e hoy'u».
  - A UNA article lists y'u among the six verbs that are irregular in their person markers.
  - I found no modern source with ahy'u. Keep hay'u; THE WATER VERB note and the Hay'use doubt can cite these sources.
- -se is tonic. Tatoeba writes it accented before atonic suffixes (Ndakaruséi, Nda'uséi, Ahasékuri, rohendusékuri), so Hay'use and Akaruse are right without an accent.
- Needs and their answers:
  - Food: Mbo'ehára, akaruse. → Ejapyhy ko mbujape. → Aguyje!
  - Bathroom and permission: Ikatúpa asẽ sapy'aite? → Héẽ, ikatu. → Aguyje, mbo'ehára.
  - Lending: Aikotevẽ mbogueha. → Ejapyhy che mbogueha. → Aguyjevete, che irũ!
  - Water has no say line of its own. «Héẽ, ikatu.» also answers «Ikatúpa hay'u?», which is enough.
- Meanings already in the app:
  - y, mbujape, haiha, mbo'ehára, irũ, Héẽ, ejapyhy, Aguyje and Aguyjevete keep their meanings.
  - kotevẽ, karu, sẽ, sapy'a and mbogue appear nowhere else in the app's data or screens. y'u appears only as the story's hoy'u, with the same meaning.
  - There are no false friends in meaning. Three sound or look-alikes are worth a check of the clips:
    - mbogueha against mbo'ehára (said twice in this unit) and mbo'ehao.
    - asẽ 'salgo' against hasẽ 'llora' (not in the app).
    - Hay-, which L2 readers may read as Spanish «hay», with a silent h.
- Spanish glosses: they are short, use voseo where a verb addresses someone (Tomá, Usá, podés), and are exact. «(al baño)» is context, as the app's other parentheses are.
- Pictures: the karu, mbogueha and ejapyhy pictures show their meanings. The toilet carries 'baño' for a phrase that does not name it, so Meet should keep the gloss visible.
- The Guarani alternatives in doubts are all grammatical and mean what they say: Ikatúpa aha hay'u?, Héẽ, tereho., Tereho ha ejevy pya'e, Aiporuka ndéve che mbogueha, Ndaguerekói mbogueha, Okañy chehegui che mbogueha, Upéi eme'ẽ jey chéve., Embojevy chéve, Mba'épa reikotevẽ?, Ikatúpa aipe'a ovetã?, Eme'ẽmína chéve kamby, Ikatúpa ha'u che chipa?. hemikotevẽ is the correct h-form (temi- before a nasal root).

One point in the notes to correct (it is not a unit string): the merge says school texts usually write the stative che apart. Tatoeba writes the stative prefixes joined: Chekane'õ, nderesarái, Ndevare'a, nekane'õrõ, nemandu'arõ. So Chey'uhéi or Cheñembyahýi could be written joined and built. verdicts.general:
Result: all 22 Guarani strings pass this lens, with no fix and no drop. Nothing in the repository was changed (git status is clean).

NEW EVIDENCE. Besides the Tatoeba copy and the MEC texts, I searched three larger corpora, downloaded read-only to my scratchpad:
- Common Voice Guarani v16 prompts, 5,893 sentences (huggingface.co/datasets/fsicoli/common_voice_16_0): dl-cv-gn/norm.txt
- Jojajovai, a Guarani–Spanish corpus of 30,855 pairs (huggingface.co/datasets/mmaguero/jojajovai). Its sources include ABC Color's Guarani edition, blogs, a seminar text, a Guarani software glossary and AmericasNLP: dl-jojajovai/allnorm.tsv
- Guarani Wikipedia plain text (huggingface.co/datasets/ffatty/plaintext-wikipedia-full-guarani): dl-gnwiki/gnwiki.norm.txt

WHAT THEY SETTLE
1. The bathroom card is attested word for word, first-hand: «Ikatúpa asẽ sapy'aite.» is a Common Voice sentence (clip 26492854 and three more). Keep the paraphrase.
   - Naming the room in Guarani does not work for children. The everyday noun is the loan baño, even in written Guarani (ABC Color Guarani «peteĩ baño clausurado»; Guarani Wikipedia «Oporandu baño-re»).
   - The Guarani nouns are learned or purist: kotyjahuha, jahuha, ñaimeha. koty'i 'cuartito' («Aha koty'ípe.») is ambiguous.
   - One correction to the notes: Guarani texts hyphenate Spanish common nouns before postpositions too, not only names («potrero-pe», «plazoleta-pe», «baño-re»). The fallback «Ikatúpa aha baño-pe?» would therefore follow written practice, but it is still a team decision. The earlier audit's rejection of «vocal-pe» concerned a word that has a Guarani equivalent (pu'ae); baño has none in common use.
2. The water verb: usage says hay'u. The corpora have hay'u, rey'u, hoy'u, jay'u, roy'u and hey'u, and the desiderative is formed exactly as on the card (Hoy'use, Roy'use). All four corpora have zero hits for hy'u (no ahy'u, rehy'u or jahy'u). Keep Hay'use and «Ikatúpa hay'u?». The audit's ahy'u, from an unverified Guasch & Ortiz citation, is at most a prescriptive variant for the Academia check.
3. karuse is attested in ABC Color Guarani («vare'a ha karuseterei»).
4. Héẽ is the dominant spelling: Common Voice has it 13 times and Hẽe never; Jojajovai has it 46 times and Hẽe once.
5. -mína is attested in 24 Common Voice lines.
6. Eiporu with a possessed object is attested: «Eiporu nde jehaiha…» in the software glossary, and «Nde ikatu reiporu che mandi'o» in Common Voice.

ATTESTATION BY STRING
- Attested whole, or nearly:
  - Aikotevẽ (as a word);
  - Ikatúpa asẽ sapy'aite? (card and say line);
  - Aguyje!;
  - Aguyje, mbo'ehára. (1.º grado);
  - Aguyjevete, che irũ! (1.º grado; Common Voice has «Aguyjetaite che irũ.»).
- Plausible, with the pattern attested:
  - night 1: Hay'use, Akaruse, the title Hay'use, akaruse, Eme'ẽmína chéve mbujape, Mbo'ehára, akaruse. and Ejapyhy ko mbujape.;
  - night 2: Ikatúpa asẽ?, Ikatúpa hay'u?, Ikatúpa akaru? and Héẽ, ikatu.;
  - night 3: Ejapyhy (title and card), Eiporu che haiha, Aikotevẽ mbogueha. and Ejapyhy che mbogueha.
- Weakest, but not doubtful enough to change: mbogueha. It is a regular school word like haiha:
  - mbogue means borrar in a Guarani software glossary;
  - mbogue + -ha also gives Wikipedia's tatambogueha 'extintor'.
  - But no corpus has it as 'borrador'.
  - It is also missing from a seminar text's list of school coinages in use (haiha, kuatiahai, aranduka, apykahai…).
  - Children mostly say borrador or goma.
  - A teacher should confirm it.

REGISTER: no needless jopara anywhere, and no purist word made up for this unit (mbogueha is a dictionary word). Every line is short, polite and sayable by a 7-year-old. Some forms teachers also use, worth noting but not changing:
- «Chevare'a» and «Chey'uhéi» for hunger and thirst. Common Voice writes both joined, but they are colloquial and are not buildable single words in the app's terms.
- «Héẽ, tereho» to let a child out.
- «sapy'ami» for 'un ratito'.

OUTSIDE THIS LENS (for the syllable lens): if ay counts as a falling diphthong, as the app counts ai in Mai·tei and hai·ha, Hay'use builds as Hay·'u·se, not Ha·y·'u·se.

MEC: no MEC text gives Guarani wording for these needs. The guide (25531b74 l.2707–2711) asks only for picture cards, example situations and practice between peers. The only related Guarani in the MEC texts is Eiporu, Eiporuporã, Jaipuru, ikatu and osẽ (88065dde l.4109 and l.1401; MAGUA guides).

LIMITS
- Common Voice prompts are sentences written by adult contributors. None of my sources is a 2.º grado Guarani textbook.
- WebFetch could not reach kaweah.freedombox.rocks (the Wiktionary mirror) or omniglot.com. Both are outside this session's network and would have to be allowed in its settings.
- GitHub access to pln-fing-udelar/jojajovai is not enabled for this session, so I used the Hugging Face copy.
- guaran-ia/gntweets and guaran-ia/kuatia on Hugging Face are gated.
- Web searches found no page with mbogueha as 'borrador', with akaruse or hay'use, or with «aha baño-pe».

words.note: y'u 'tomar agua' (y 'agua' + 'u) with -se 'quiero'. -se is tonic, so there is no accent (Tatoeba «Ha'use…», «Ndakaruséi», «Ahasékuri»). y'u conjugates like 'u (ha'u, re'u, ho'u; imperative he'u): hay'u, rey'u, hoy'u, imperative hey'u. The corpora have these forms, with -se as here (Common Voice «hay'u ha aguapy…», «Rey'u hag̃ua.», «Roy'usemínteko ikatumírõ.», «Hoy'usetereíningo.»; Tatoeba «Hey'u.», «che hay'urã»), and none has ahy'u (see THE WATER VERB). The app's story has hoy'u. Ha·y·'u·se: y is its own syllable, as in y·pe. Guarani Wikipedia's article on vowel groups lists no vowel + y diphthong and splits Pa·ra·gua·y (see SYLLABLES OF HAY'USE and doubts). The picture is unit 2's water drop, and the y of 'agua' is inside the word.

final.notes:
THE VERIFICATION (this step)
- Three lenses checked all 22 Guarani strings: spelling and syllables; meaning and grammar; and usage, register and attestation. Every string passed every lens. No string needed a fix or a drop.
  - The unit's Guarani, glosses, pictures and syllables are the merge's, unchanged, so «changes» is empty.
- The lenses differed on one point, the syllables of Hay'use.
  - The spelling lens gives Ha·y·'u·se. The usage lens asked about Hay·'u·se, in case ay is a diphthong.
  - Ha·y·'u·se has the stronger evidence and is kept (see SYLLABLES OF HAY'USE and doubts).
- The lenses corrected four points in the merge's notes. The corrections are applied below:
  1. 'u conjugates ha'u, re'u, ho'u, with he'u as the imperative; the merge had written «ha'u, he'u, ho'u». So y'u is hay'u, rey'u, hoy'u, imperative hey'u.
  2. The stative che is not usually written apart. The corpora mostly write it joined:
     - Common Voice: «Chevare'a.», «Chey'uhéi.», «Chekane'õ», «Cherasy»;
     - Tatoeba: «Ndevare'a piko?», «Chekane'õ.».
     - Only a few lines write it apart (Common Voice «Che vare'aitereíkuri.»).
     - The merge's claim is removed; its other reasons for the -se pair stand.
  3. Guarani texts hyphenate Spanish common nouns before a postposition, not only foreign names: «potrero-pe» (Common Voice), «plazoleta-pe» (ABC Color's Guarani edition), «Oporandu baño-re» (Guarani Wikipedia).
  4. The bathroom sentence is now attested first-hand, word for word, in Common Voice.
- The water verb is settled by usage: hay'u (see THE WATER VERB).
- I read every corpus line cited in these notes in the local copies (see EVIDENCE AND LIMITS).

THE MERGE
Most of the unit is kept as both drafts wrote it:
- the title Aikotevẽ and the three night titles;
- the bathroom card «Ikatúpa asẽ sapy'aite?» on a new toilet picture;
- the Ikatúpa frame for water and food;
- the food request «Eme'ẽmína chéve…»;
- the card Ejapyhy on a new handing picture;
- eiporu and aikotevẽ in night 3;
- the say lines «Ejapyhy ko mbujape.» and «Aguyje!».
Where the drafts differed:
- Night 1's needs come from draft 2: the pair Hay'use / Akaruse.
  - Each is one word, both can be built, and both end in -se 'quiero'.
  - Their verbs come back in night 2's «Ikatúpa hay'u?» and «Ikatúpa akaru?».
  - Draft 1's Chey'uhéi / Chevare'a were not kept. vare'a is colloquial (ñembyahýi is the school word), and they do not link to night 2.
  - The first person comes from draft 1: hay'u, not draft 2's ahy'u (see THE WATER VERB).
- Akaruse gets a new picture: a child with a spoon and an empty bowl.
  - Draft 2 used bread, which made 'comer' look like 'pan'.
  - The new picture also replaces draft 1's hungry child (vare'a), which risked reading as a tummy ache.
- The food request asks for mbujape (draft 1): both drafts use the word, and the say set hands over bread.
- Night 2's third card is «Ikatúpa akaru?» (draft 2), not «Ikatúpa ha'u che chipa?» (draft 1). It is shorter, and it does not sound like «Ikatúpa hay'u?».
- Night 2's say set is draft 1's need, answer and thanks.
  - «Héẽ, ikatu.» answers all three Ikatúpa cards.
  - «Aguyje, mbo'ehára.» closes it, as in 1.º grado.
- Night 3's cards come from draft 1: mbogueha, Ejapyhy and Eiporu che haiha.
  - They show three different objects, so the pictures stay apart.
  - Draft 2's Eiporu card (a child writing) was its weakest picture.
- Night 3's dialogue lends the eraser and ends with thanks: Aikotevẽ mbogueha. / Ejapyhy che mbogueha. / Aguyjevete, che irũ!
  - The first line takes draft 2's plain object (no peteĩ).
  - The last line is 1.º grado's own, with draft 2's Aguyjevete and che irũ. It names the classmate.
  - Every say line is 21 graphemes or fewer. Mborevi'i's speech bubble in Say does not wrap (white-space: nowrap), and the app's longest say line now is 25.

THE UNIT
- Night 1 «Hay'use, akaruse»: the merienda, with the teacher.
  - Needs: tomar agua (Hay'use) and pedir alimentos (Akaruse; Eme'ẽmína chéve mbujape).
  - Say: Mbo'ehára, akaruse. / Ejapyhy ko mbujape. / Aguyje!
- Night 2 «Ikatúpa asẽ?»: in class, with the teacher.
  - Needs: ir al baño and solicitar permiso, all in 1.º grado's frame Ikatúpa + a-verb?: asẽ sapy'aite (bathroom), hay'u (water), akaru (eating).
  - Say: Ikatúpa asẽ sapy'aite? / Héẽ, ikatu. / Aguyje, mbo'ehára.
- Night 3 «Ejapyhy»: in class, between classmates.
  - Need: prestar algo, with the child as the lender.
  - Cards: mbogueha, Ejapyhy, Eiporu che haiha.
  - Say: Aikotevẽ mbogueha. / Ejapyhy che mbogueha. / Aguyjevete, che irũ!

THE MEC
- Priorización curricular 2021, Comunicación Guaraní, 2.º grado, item 16 (p. 28, docs/mec-check.json): «Expresa necesidades básicas como: ir al baño, tomar agua, pedir alimentos, solicitar permiso y prestar algo.»
  - The same sentence is in the Programa de estudio, 2.º grado, Segunda lengua (mec-text/7e820984…, p. 57).
- Guía para la planificación 2021, 2.º grado, week 4 «Necesidades básicas» (mec-text/25531b74…, l. 2707–2711). It asks for picture cards of the needs, example situations and practice between peers.
- No MEC text gives Guarani wording for these needs. The Priorización's own Guarani text calls needs hemikotevẽ, the noun of the title's verb.
- All five needs are on cards, not only in say lines, because L1 children play no Say in 2.º grado (tp-course.js, gamesFor):
  - ir al baño: «Ikatúpa asẽ sapy'aite?»
  - tomar agua: Hay'use, «Ikatúpa hay'u?»
  - pedir alimentos: Akaruse, «Eme'ẽmína chéve mbujape»
  - solicitar permiso: the three Ikatúpa cards
  - prestar algo: Ejapyhy, «Eiporu che haiha»
- How the guide's activities appear:
  - Picture cards: the Meet, Pick and Read games.
  - Situations: the three scenes.
  - Practice between peers: night 3, and Say, where the child says both roles.

BUILT ON 1.º GRADO UNIT 5 AND 2.º GRADO UNIT 2 (no card repeated)
- Ikatúpa + a-verb? gets three new verbs: asẽ (the opposite of aike), hay'u and akaru.
- Eme'ẽmína chéve… now asks for food: mbujape instead of kuatia.
- ejapyhy moves from a say line («Héẽ, ejapyhy.») to a card, and now the child is the one who hands over.
- «Ikatúpa aiporu nde haiha?» becomes «Eiporu che haiha»: the child lends its own pencil.
- Three say lines are 1.º grado's own: «Aguyje!», «Aguyje, mbo'ehára.» and «Aguyjevete, che irũ!».
- Reused words keep their app meanings: y 'agua' (the water drop, and inside hay'u), mbujape 'pan', haiha 'lápiz', mbo'ehára, irũ, Héẽ, Aguyje, Aguyjevete.
- New grammar is small: the desiderative -se (Hay'use, Akaruse) and aikotevẽ, the title verb.

THE BATHROOM QUESTION
Choice: the Guarani paraphrase «Ikatúpa asẽ sapy'aite?» (¿Puedo salir un ratito?), on a new toilet picture, glossed «¿Puedo salir un ratito? (al baño)». Both drafts chose it independently, and all three lenses kept it. Reasons:
1. The sentence is attested word for word.
   - «Ikatúpa asẽ sapy'aite.» is a validated sentence of Common Voice Guarani v16 (clip common_voice_gn_26492854, and three more recordings in its «other» set), read in the local copy.
   - The Paraguayan civil-service course «Guaraní Comunicativo en la Función Pública» has it as a polite permission request (search summary, docs/unit5-check.json).
   - Its parts are everyday Guarani:
     - asẽ: Tatoeba «Asẽkuri javete»;
     - sapy'aite: Common Voice «Asẽta sapy'aite.», and a blog in Jojajovai «Eha'arõmína sapy'aite»;
     - the frame Ikatúpa, which mirrors 1.º grado's «Ikatúpa aike?».
2. The everyday noun is the Spanish loan, even in written Guarani.
   - ABC Color's Guarani edition writes «peteĩ baño clausurado» (Jojajovai), and Guarani Wikipedia «Oporandu baño-re».
   - Wikipedia's Jopara article gives «Mo'o opyta baño?» as its example of mixed speech (search summary).
   - In the MEC texts, baño appears only in Spanish.
3. The Guarani nouns are learned compounds, not child vocabulary.
   - kotyjahuha occurs (Common Voice «Aike kotyjahuhápe ha ajovahéi.»; a blog in Jojajovai, for 'baño' in a sanitation text).
   - jahuha and ñaimeha appear in a list of house rooms in Guarani Wikipedia.
   - koty'i 'cuartito' («Aha koty'ípe.», Common Voice) is ambiguous.
   - Putting one on a card for 7-year-olds would be the purist choice the brief rules out.
4. The loan needs a team decision before it goes on a card.
   - b is not a letter of the achegety; it appears only inside mb.
   - The app's audit (docs/guarani-audit.json, g313) advised against «Mba'e vocal-pe oñepyrũ?», which mixes in a Spanish word. vocal has a Guarani equivalent (pu'ae), while baño has none in common use, so that ruling does not settle this case either way.
5. «¿Puedo salir?» is how Paraguayan children politely ask for the bathroom in Spanish too. The picture and the gloss name the place, which is what the guide's picture cards ask for.
6. Guarani's own verb for the need, kuaru 'orinar' (akuaruse), names a body function rather than asking politely, and no school or phrase source used it. It is not used.
Fallback, if teachers want the room named: «Ikatúpa aha baño-pe?», which is what most families say. The lenses differ on how to write it:
- The usage lens writes baño-pe, as written Guarani does with Spanish nouns before a postposition (baño-re, plazoleta-pe, potrero-pe).
- The spelling lens would guaranize it as váñope: v for b as in Tatoeba's «Víno», an acute for the stress, and -pe joined. But no source writes váño.
- Written practice has the stronger evidence, so baño-pe would be the form. Either way, putting a Spanish noun on a Guarani card needs a team decision, and the line needs a new clip.

THE WATER VERB
y'u 'tomar agua' conjugates like 'u (ha'u, re'u, ho'u; imperative he'u): hay'u, rey'u, hoy'u, jay'u, roy'u, pey'u; imperative hey'u. All three lenses keep hay'u. Evidence:
- Corpora, read locally:
  - Common Voice: «hay'u ha aguapy peteĩ nangiriju ári.», «Rey'u hag̃ua.», «Roy'usemínteko ikatumírõ.», «Hoy'usetereíningo.» (the last two with -se, as on the card);
  - Guarani Wikipedia: «Aníke jakaru ha jay'u heta tapicha apytépe…»;
  - Tatoeba: «Hey'u.» beside «He'u!», and «Eme'ẽ chéve che hay'urã.».
  - None of the four corpora (Common Voice, Jojajovai, Guarani Wikipedia, Tatoeba) has a form with hy'u: no ahy'u, rehy'u or jahy'u.
- By search summary:
  - Ávalos' dictionary and a UNLP Guarani course page: «Che hay'u, nde rey'u, ha'e hoy'u»;
  - the GuaraniAyvuWeb dictionary and a Corrientes verb list;
  - English Wikipedia ('a'y'u is pronounced hay'u) and the USC Guarani Corpus (hay'ú, 1Sg.drink);
  - a UNA article that lists y'u among the six verbs irregular in their person markers.
- Against it:
  - The app's audit (docs/guarani-audit.json, g290) gave ahy'u, rehy'u, hoy'u from Guasch & Ortiz, without a quote, and one of its reviewers gave ay'u.
  - No one in this work could open that dictionary.
  - The app itself writes only the third person hoy'u (tp-sky.js), which every paradigm shares.

SYLLABLES OF HAY'USE
- Kept: Ha·y·'u·se (spelling lens).
  - a + y is not counted as a diphthong, so y is a syllable of its own, as in the app's y·pe.
  - The tiles also show L2 readers that y is the Guarani vowel, not part of the Spanish «hay».
- Evidence: Guarani Wikipedia's article on vowel groups, «Pu'ae aty guaraníme» by David Galeano Olivera.
  - It counts y among the weak vowels, but its list of diphthongs has no vowel + y. The list is ai, ei, oi, ui, au, eu, ua, ue, ia, ie, ya, yi and their nasal forms.
  - It gives ay in Pa·ra·gua·y and oy in mbo·y as hiatus.
  - The app's own diphthongs are all of the kinds on that list: Mai·tei, Mba·'éi, hai·ha, Ei·chu, mo·kõi, ta·pỹi, kua·ra·hy.
- The usage lens asked about Hay·'u·se, in case ay is a falling diphthong like ai. No source treats it so. The question is recorded in doubts.

PICTURES
- Existing: y (Hay'use, «Ikatúpa hay'u?»), mbujape, haiha.
- New, 4 (the maximum): karu (Akaruse and «Ikatúpa akaru?»), baño, mbogueha, ejapyhy. None of these keys is in tp-pics.js yet.
- The scratch worktree (scratchpad/wt) already draws baño and ejapyhy.
  - Its ejapyhy hands over a yellow pencil, which next to «Eiporu che haiha» would look like the pencil card.
  - So the new picture hands over a blue notebook; the drawn hands can stay.
- y and karu each appear in two nights (the need, then the permission), never twice in one night. The engine never puts two options with the same picture side by side.

doubts.doubt: The card asks «¿puedo salir un ratito?». Only the toilet picture and the gloss «(al baño)» name the bathroom, so Meet must show the gloss, and an L2 child may take asẽ itself to mean 'baño'. The sentence is attested word for word: it is a validated Common Voice sentence, and the Función Pública course has it (by search summary). Both are adult sources, not children's texts. Most families, and many teachers, say the jopara «Ikatúpa aha baño-pe?». That fallback needs a team decision, because b is not a letter of the achegety, and the lenses disagree on its spelling. The usage lens would write baño-pe, as written Guarani does with Spanish nouns before a postposition (Guarani Wikipedia «Oporandu baño-re», «plazoleta-pe», «potrero-pe»). The spelling lens would guaranize it as váñope (v for b as in Tatoeba's «Víno», an acute for the stress), but no source writes váño. Written practice has the stronger evidence. The shorter «Ikatúpa asẽ?» (an exact mirror of «Ikatúpa aike?») and «sapy'ami» (Tatoeba «Epytu'úna sapy'ami.») are also natural; the meaning and usage lenses both keep the attested sapy'aite. sapy'a alone can mean 'de repente', though not in a permission request. A Guarani teacher should confirm which form 2.º grado classrooms use. Check the clip: the voice has garbled short nasal words, and asẽ 'salgo' must not sound like hasẽ 'llora'. The gloss (33 characters) is longer than any card gloss now (29).

All three lenses keep hay'u, and the evidence is now strong. The corpora have hay'u, rey'u, hoy'u, jay'u, roy'u and hey'u, with -se attached as here (Common Voice «Roy'usemínteko», «Hoy'usetereíningo»). None of the four corpora (Common Voice, Jojajovai, Guarani Wikipedia, Tatoeba) has ahy'u, rehy'u or jahy'u. Dictionaries and courses found by search summary agree: Ávalos and a UNLP Guarani course («Che hay'u, nde rey'u, ha'e hoy'u»), GuaraniAyvuWeb, a Corrientes verb list, English Wikipedia and the USC corpus. The only source against it is the app's own audit (docs/guarani-audit.json, g290), which gave ahy'u, rehy'u, hoy'u from Guasch & Ortiz without a quote; one of its reviewers gave ay'u. Nobody could open that dictionary. If the Academia ever prescribes ahy'u, change three things together: Hay'use → Ahy'use (A·hy·'u·se), «Ikatúpa hay'u?» → «Ikatúpa ahy'u?», and the night 1 title. Every form keeps the story's hoy'u. An L2 child may read «Hay» as the Spanish «hay», with a silent h; the clip models the [h].

Syllables: the spelling lens gives Ha·y·'u·se: a + y is not a diphthong, so y is its own syllable, as in the app's y·pe. The usage lens asked whether it should be Hay·'u·se, if ay counts as a falling diphthong, as ai does in the app's Mai·tei and hai·ha. Ha·y·'u·se is kept. Guarani Wikipedia's article on vowel groups («Pu'ae aty guaraníme», by David Galeano Olivera) counts y among the weak vowels, but its list of diphthongs has no vowel + y, and it gives ay in Pa·ra·gua·y and oy in mbo·y as hiatus. Its two examples have the stress on y, while Hay'use is stressed on se, and I found no source that splits an unstressed ay (as in hay'u or mborayhu). A Guarani teacher should confirm how children are taught to split it. Either split joins back to the word, so a change would touch only syl.

For the needs themselves, the statives «Chey'uhéi» (tengo sed) and «Chevare'a» or «Che ñembyahýi» (tengo hambre) are at least as common as Hay'use and Akaruse. Common Voice writes «Chey'uhéi.» and «Chevare'a.» joined, so they could be built as words. The merge's claim that school texts write the stative che apart did not hold up: only a few lines write it apart, such as «Che vare'aitereíkuri.». The statives are left out for two reasons. vare'a is colloquial (ñembyahýi is the school word). And Hay'use and Akaruse share their verbs with night 2's «Ikatúpa hay'u?» and «Ikatúpa akaru?», which links the need to the permission. If the team prefers the statives, change the cards, the night 1 title and the first say line together, and settle their syllables. Akaruse's new picture must read as 'quiero comer' next to the bread of «Eme'ẽmína chéve mbujape». If it cannot, draft 2's choice needs no new picture: unit 2's bread for Akaruse, and «Eme'ẽmína chéve kamby» for the request.

Every two-item night title in the app joins its items with ha («Chipa ha mandi'o», «Y ha kamby», «Okẽ ha ovetã»). Those are pairs of nouns, and this title is two wishes, so the comma works, as in the app's «Pyhareve, ka'aru, pyhare». If the team wants the ha pattern, the title would be «Hay'use ha akaruse». It changes with the cards if hay'u ever does.

-mína is spelled as in 1.º grado and is common (24 Common Voice lines; Tatoeba writes -míkena). The Academia's spelling of its accent is still to be confirmed app-wide. Draft 2 asked for kamby, the milk of the merienda escolar. mbujape is kept because both drafts use it and the say set hands over bread. With a classmate, children more often say «Eme'ẽmi chéve…» or the jopara «convidame». Guarani has no article, so the gloss says «pan».

When the water is outside the room, a child asks to go: «Ikatúpa aha hay'u?» (¿Puedo ir a tomar agua?). The card keeps the frame's shorter form, which is natural with a bottle on the desk. Its spelling follows Hay'use (see that doubt). Water has no say line of its own; «Héẽ, ikatu.» answers it too.

It repeats night 1's karu on purpose (the need, then the permission), as «Ikatúpa hay'u?» repeats y'u. Draft 1's «Ikatúpa ha'u che chipa?» (¿Puedo comer mi chipá?) reuses unit 2's chipa, but it is longer (23), and next to «Ikatúpa hay'u?» it sounds close (ha'u / hay'u). Children also ask to eat less often than they ask for the bathroom or water. If the team wants a permission that is not about the body, «Ikatúpa aipe'a ovetã?» (¿Puedo abrir la ventana?, picture ovetã) fits the slot.

It is the plain answer to Ikatúpa…?, and it fits all three cards of the night. A teacher letting a child out often says «Héẽ, tereho.» (Sí, andá; Tatoeba has «Tereho ko'ãga.»). Draft 1 suggested «Tereho ha ejevy pya'e» (andá y volvé rápido), left out to keep the line short. Héẽ keeps 1.º grado's spelling and is by far the commoner written form: 13 to 0 against Hẽe in Common Voice, and 38 to 1 in Jojajovai's Guarani. But Tatoeba has both, and the Academia's entry is still to be confirmed app-wide. Check the clip: the voice has garbled short nasal words.

It is the weakest word of the unit. It is kept because it is a regular word of the haiha kind, and no better non-Spanish word turned up. Its meaning 'borrador' rests on search summaries only. The spelling lens found David Galeano Olivera's lesson for children («Borrador es mbogueha») and a Paraguayan school plan («Mbogueha (Borrador)»), and draft 1 found the Argentine Avañe'ẽ dictionary. My searches in this step could not find those pages again. None of the four corpora has it as 'borrador'. A seminar text's list of school words in use (haiha, kuatiahai, aranduka, apykahai…) leaves it out, though that list ends «y varios otros». Many children just say «borrador» or «goma». mboje'oha is the dictionary's other form. It sounds a little like mbo'ehára, which this unit says twice, and like mbo'ehao, so check the clip. A Guarani teacher should confirm it is the school word.

eipyhy (from pyhy) is also heard (Common Voice «Eipyhy pe ajaka…»). This hand-over use is natural, and 1.º grado already has «Héẽ, ejapyhy.», but the corpora have japyhy only in other senses. The scratch worktree's ejapyhy picture hands over a yellow pencil, which next to «Eiporu che haiha» would look like the pencil card, so swap the pencil for a notebook. A handing picture is somewhat abstract: check that children read it as 'tomá'. Lending is said with everyday verbs (tomá, usá), not with poruka, which 1.º grado's check found only in dictionaries. Families also say the jopara «ambopresta». If the team wants the verb 'prestar' itself: «Aiporuka ndéve che mbogueha» (Te presto mi borrador), with ndéve for the receiver.

«Usá mi lápiz» lends by letting someone use the pencil, which is how children lend, but the verb is 'usar', not 'prestar' (see Ejapyhy). Tatoeba writes puru (aipuru), while the MEC guides write Eiporu and the app aiporu, so I kept poru; some children will say «Eipuru». L1 children play no Say in 2.º grado, so they meet aikotevẽ only in the unit title. Draft 2's card «Aikotevẽ haiha» (Necesito un lápiz) could take this slot if the team wants the title verb on a card.

In Tatoeba, aikotevẽ takes a plain object («Opavave oikotevẽ pirapire») and also -re («oikotevẽ ikafére»); Common Voice has «Aikotevẽ terere.». Draft 1 said «Aikotevẽ peteĩ mbogueha.» (un borrador), which is just as natural but longer. A child may just as well say «Ndaguerekói mbogueha» (No tengo borrador) or «Okañy chehegui che mbogueha» (Perdí mi borrador; Tatoeba has it with haiha). The voice has trouble with final nasals (aikotevẽ), so check the clip.

Draft 1 ended the dialogue with «Upéi eme'ẽ jey chéve.» (Después me lo devolvés), which makes it a loan rather than a gift. That line is unattested as a whole (built from upéi, jey as in «Eha'ã jey», eme'ẽ and chéve), and «Embojevy chéve» is the other form. The merge keeps the thank-you, as every dialogue of 1.º grado unit 5 ends, and lets «Eiporu che haiha» carry the loan. This line is 1.º grado's own, so it repeats a say line, not a card.

«Maestra» follows the app's gloss of mbo'ehára; children often say «Profe». mbo'ehára and irũ have no gender, so «maestra» and «amiga» could just as well be «maestro» and «amigo». A teacher who models politeness may prefer the permission form «Mbo'ehára, ikatúpa akaru?», which night 2 teaches. This line states the need, as item 16 asks.

Other possible unit titles: «Mba'épa reikotevẽ?» (¿Qué necesitás?, the teacher's question) or the MEC's own noun: the Priorización's Guarani text writes hemikotevẽ. As a word, Aikotevẽ is said only in night 3's first say line.
